decks.title: Measurements and Experimentation — Part 1: Units and least count
goals: Name the seven fundamental SI quantities with their units and express derived units in them
Convert a quantity between SI, cgs and fps units
Find the least count of a rule, measuring cylinder and stopwatch and explain why a smaller least count means greater accuracy

slides.heading: Measuring is comparing
slides.body_md: Part 1 — every measurement compares a quantity with an agreed unit, and every instrument can only be read to a certain smallest step.

visual.alt: Flow: quantity, unit, instrument, reading

slides.narration: To measure anything we need a unit to compare with and an instrument to do the comparing. In this part we meet the international system of units and learn what limits the accuracy of an instrument.

slides.heading: The seven fundamental SI quantities
slides.body_md: The **International System of Units (SI)** is built on seven **fundamental quantities**. Each has one **fundamental unit**.

visual.alt: Table of the seven fundamental SI quantities with their units and symbols

slides.narration: Length is measured in metres, mass in kilograms and time in seconds. Electric current uses the ampere, temperature the kelvin, luminous intensity the candela and amount of substance the mole. Every other unit is built from these seven.

slides.heading: Derived units
slides.body_md: A **derived unit** is made by combining fundamental units. Force, work and pressure have their own names, but each can be written with kilogram, metre and second.

visual.alt: Table of derived quantities, their formulae and units in fundamental units

slides.narration: Density is mass divided by volume, so its unit is kilogram per cubic metre. Momentum is mass times velocity, so its unit is kilogram metre per second. Always work out a derived unit by following the formula.

slides.heading: Quick check: fundamental or derived
slides.body_md: Think about which quantities need a combination of other units.

visual.alt: Table of four quantities and their units

slides.narration: Look at the four quantities in the table. Which unit is not a fundamental SI unit?

slides.heading: Three systems of units
slides.body_md: Besides SI there are the **cgs** system (centimetre, gram, second) and the **fps** system (foot, pound, second).

visual.alt: Table comparing the base units of the SI, cgs and fps systems

slides.narration: All three systems measure time in seconds. They differ in the units of length and mass. Science and the ICSE syllabus use SI, but older books and some machines still use the other two.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: converting units
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Convert (a) a cycling speed of 54 km per hour to m per second and (b) an oil density of 0.8 g per cm³ to kg per m³.

**Step 1.** $1\ \text{km} = 1000\ \text{m}$ and $1\ \text{h} = 3600\ \text{s}$, so 54 km per hour is $\dfrac{54 \times 1000}{3600} = 15$ m per second.

**Step 2.** $1\ \text{g} = 10^{-3}\ \text{kg}$ and $1\ \text{cm}^3 = 10^{-6}\ \text{m}^3$, so $1\ \text{g cm}^{-3} = 1000\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$.

**Step 3.** $0.8 \times 1000 = 800$ kg per m³.

visual.alt: Table showing the conversion of a speed and a density to SI units

slides.narration: Write the conversion factor first, then multiply. A kilometre is a thousand metres and an hour is three thousand six hundred seconds, so a speed in kilometres per hour is divided by three point six. A density in grams per cubic centimetre is multiplied by one thousand.

slides.body_md: Use the factor from the worked example.

slides.heading: Least count
slides.body_md: The **least count** of an instrument is the **smallest value it can measure accurately**. For a scale it equals the value of one smallest division.

headers: How the least count is found
rows: volume between two marks ÷ divisions between them
time of one revolution ÷ divisions on the dial

visual.alt: Table showing how to find the least count of a rule, a measuring cylinder and a stopwatch

slides.narration: The least count is the value of one smallest division. A metre rule has millimetre divisions, so its least count is one millimetre. For a measuring cylinder, divide the volume between two numbered marks by the number of divisions between them.

slides.heading: Reading a measuring cylinder
slides.body_md: Between the **40** and **50** mark there are **5** divisions, so each division is $\dfrac{10}{5} = 2$ mL. The water level is **3 divisions** above 40.

slides.narration: First find the least count. Ten millilitres are shared among five divisions, so each is two millilitres. The level is three divisions above forty, so the reading is forty six millilitres. Read with your eye level with the surface.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: least count of a cylinder and a stopwatch
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** (a) A cylinder is marked 0 to 100 mL with 40 divisions. (b) A stopwatch dial has 300 divisions for one turn of 60 s. Find both least counts.

**Step 1.** Cylinder: $\dfrac{100}{40} = 2.5$ mL.

**Step 2.** Stopwatch: $\dfrac{60}{300} = 0.2$ s.

**Step 3.** A reading can be trusted only to these steps.

visual.alt: Table of the least counts of a cylinder and a stopwatch

slides.narration: Divide the range by the number of divisions. The cylinder gives two point five millilitres. The stopwatch gives zero point two seconds. You cannot read either instrument more finely than this.

slides.heading: Quick check: finding a least count
slides.body_md: Count the divisions between the two marks.

visual.alt: Table giving the marks of a measuring cylinder and the divisions between them

slides.narration: Between the twenty and thirty millilitre marks there are five divisions. What is the least count?

slides.heading: Smaller least count, greater accuracy
slides.body_md: A ball dropped from 2.0 m takes about **0.63 s** to land (g = 10 m s⁻²). A stopwatch that reads only to 0.1 s could be wrong by 16% of this time; one that reads to 0.01 s by only 1.6%.

headers: As a fraction of the time

visual.alt: Table comparing the possible error of a coarse and a fine stopwatch

slides.narration: The smaller the least count, the smaller the possible error compared with the measurement. That is why a stopwatch that reads to a hundredth of a second gives a more accurate time than one that reads to a tenth.

slides.body_md: Compare the least counts before you decide.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Seven fundamental SI quantities: length, mass, time, current, temperature, luminous intensity, amount of substance.
A derived unit is built from fundamental units, for example kg m⁻³ for density.
SI, cgs and fps differ in the units of length and mass; 1 g cm⁻³ = 1000 kg m⁻³.
Least count is the smallest value an instrument reads; a smaller least count means greater accuracy.

visual.alt: Summary table of the key conversions and the least count rule

slides.narration: To sum up. There are seven fundamental quantities. Derived units are combinations of them. Convert with care, using the factor for each unit. And the smaller the least count, the more accurate the instrument.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Write the unit with every answer; a number without a unit loses the mark.
Write the conversion factor first, then substitute.
To find a least count, state the range and the number of divisions.
Give the unit of a derived quantity in fundamental units when asked.

slides.narration: Exam tips. Always write units. Show the conversion factor. When finding a least count, count the gaps between marks and not the marks themselves.

slides.heading: Vernier callipers and its least count
slides.body_md: A **Vernier callipers** has a **main scale** and a sliding **vernier scale**. Ten vernier divisions are equal to nine main scale divisions (1 MSD = 1 mm), so one vernier division is 0.9 mm and the **least count is 0.1 mm = 0.01 cm**.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: reading a Vernier callipers
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Read the diameter of the cylinder from the figure.

**Step 1.** Main scale reading (just before the vernier zero): 23 mm.

**Step 2.** Vernier line that coincides with a main scale line: the **4th**.

**Step 3.** Vernier reading $= 4 \times 0.1 = 0.4$ mm.

**Step 4.** Reading $= 23 + 0.4 = 23.4$ mm $= 2.34$ cm.

slides.heading: Zero error of a Vernier callipers
slides.body_md: With the jaws **closed** the zero of the vernier should meet the zero of the main scale. If it does not, the instrument has a **zero error**. Here the vernier zero is to the right and the 3rd line coincides: zero error = **+0.03 cm**. For a positive error, **subtract** it. If the vernier zero is to the left, the error is negative and is **added**.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: correcting a reading
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** The jaws of this Vernier callipers show a zero error of $+0.03$ cm. The figure shows the reading for a cylinder. Find its true diameter.

**Step 1.** Main scale reading 14 mm and the 8th vernier line coincides, so the observed reading is $14 + 8 \times 0.1 = 14.8$ mm $= 1.48$ cm.

**Step 2.** True reading = observed reading − zero error $= 1.48 - 0.03 = 1.45$ cm.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: reading a screw gauge
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Read the diameter of the wire. (Pitch 1 mm, 100 divisions.)

**Step 1.** Linear scale reading: 5 mm.

**Step 2.** Circular scale division on the datum line: 37, so $37 \times 0.01 = 0.37$ mm.

**Step 3.** Reading $= 5 + 0.37 = 5.37$ mm.

slides.body_md: A **simple pendulum** is a small heavy bob on a light thread. The **time period T** is the time for **one complete oscillation** (A to B to A to C to A) and the **frequency f** is the number of oscillations per second, so **f = 1/T**. The unit of T is the second and of f is the hertz.

slides.narration: One complete oscillation is a trip from the mean position to one extreme, back through the mean position to the other extreme and back again. The time for this is the period. The frequency is the number of oscillations in one second, which is the reciprocal of the period.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: the time period formula
slides.body_md:
The time period of a simple pendulum of effective length $l$ is $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g}}$ (given without derivation). It does not depend on the mass of the bob.

**Problem.** Find T for $l = 2.5$ m. (Take $\pi = 3.14$ and $g = 10$ m s⁻².)

**Step 1.** $T = 2 \times 3.14 \times \sqrt{\dfrac{2.5}{10}} = 6.28 \times 0.5 = 3.14$ s.

rows: Taken to a place with smaller g

slides.narration: Put the length and g into the formula. Two point five divided by ten is one quarter, whose square root is one half. The period is two times pi times one half, which is about three point one four seconds. The mass of the bob has no effect.

slides.heading: Quick check: effect of length
slides.body_md: T is proportional to the square root of the length.

slides.heading: The l against T² graph
slides.body_md: Squaring gives $T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{g}\,l$, so a graph of **l (y-axis) against T² (x-axis)** is a **straight line through the origin**. Its slope $= \dfrac{\Delta l}{\Delta T^2} = \dfrac{g}{4\pi^2}$, so **g = 4π² × slope**. Here the slope is 0.25 m s⁻², so g = 4 × 3.14² × 0.25 = 9.86 m s⁻².

sections.heading: 1. International System of Units
sections.body_md:
Measuring a physical quantity means comparing it with a standard called a **unit**. The **SI** (International System of Units) is built on seven **fundamental quantities**.

| Quantity | SI unit | Symbol |
|---|---|---|
| Length | metre | m |
| Mass | kilogram | kg |
| Time | second | s |
| Electric current | ampere | A |
| Temperature | kelvin | K |
| Luminous intensity | candela | cd |
| Amount of substance | mole | mol |

A **derived unit** is obtained from the fundamental units by following the formula of the quantity: density = mass ÷ volume gives kg m⁻³; momentum = mass × velocity gives kg m s⁻¹; force = mass × acceleration gives kg m s⁻² (the newton).

**Other systems.** In the **cgs** system the units of length, mass and time are the centimetre, gram and second; in the **fps** system they are the foot, pound and second.

**Conversions** used in this chapter: 1 km h⁻¹ = 1000 ÷ 3600 m s⁻¹ (so 54 km h⁻¹ = 15 m s⁻¹); 1 g cm⁻³ = 1000 kg m⁻³ (so 0.8 g cm⁻³ = 800 kg m⁻³); 1 lb = 0.4536 kg; 1 ft = 30.48 cm.

key_terms.definition_md: The unit of one of the seven fundamental quantities; it cannot be expressed in other units.
A unit obtained by combining fundamental units according to the formula of the quantity.

sections.heading: 2. Least count
sections.body_md:
The **least count** (LC) of an instrument is the **smallest value that it can measure accurately**. For a scale it is the value of one smallest division.

| Instrument | Least count |
|---|---|
| Metre rule | 1 mm = 0.1 cm |
| Measuring cylinder | (volume between two marks) ÷ (divisions between them), for example 10 mL ÷ 5 = 2 mL |
| Stopwatch | (time of one turn of the pointer) ÷ (divisions on the dial) |

A measurement can be trusted only up to the least count. An instrument with a **smaller least count** gives a **more accurate** measurement, because the possible error is a smaller fraction of the quantity measured.

Read a measuring cylinder with the eye level with the **bottom of the meniscus** of water.

key_terms.definition_md: The smallest value that an instrument can measure accurately.

sections.heading: 3. Vernier callipers
sections.body_md:
A **Vernier callipers** measures lengths, diameters and thicknesses to 0.1 mm. It has a **main scale** (1 MSD = 1 mm) and a sliding **vernier scale** in which **10 vernier divisions = 9 main scale divisions**.

**Least count** = 1 MSD − 1 VSD = 1 mm − 0.9 mm = **0.1 mm = 0.01 cm** (in general, LC = 1 MSD ÷ number of vernier divisions).

**Reading.** (1) Note the main scale reading (MSR) just before the vernier zero. (2) Find the vernier line (n) that coincides with a main scale line. (3) Reading = MSR + n × LC. Example: 23 mm + 4 × 0.1 mm = 23.4 mm = 2.34 cm.

**Zero error.** Close the jaws. If the vernier zero is **to the right** of the main zero, the error is **positive** (observed readings are too large), equal to (coinciding line) × LC, and the **correction is subtracted**. If the vernier zero is **to the left**, the error is **negative**, equal to −(10 − n) × LC, and it is **added**. True reading = observed reading − zero error.

Only pictorial readings are asked in this course: read the scale in the figure, as in the diagrams.

key_terms.definition_md: The reading shown by the instrument when it should read zero, such as with the jaws closed.
The least count of a Vernier callipers: the difference between one main scale division and one vernier division.

sections.heading: 4. Micrometre screw gauge
sections.body_md:
A **screw gauge** measures the diameter of a thin wire or the thickness of a sheet to 0.01 mm. Its parts are the **anvil, spindle, sleeve** (linear scale, with the datum line), **thimble** (circular scale) and **ratchet** (which prevents the spindle being tightened too much).

**Pitch** = distance moved by the spindle in one full turn of the thimble = **1 mm** here. **Least count = pitch ÷ number of circular scale divisions = 1 mm ÷ 100 = 0.01 mm**.

**Reading** = linear scale reading + (circular scale division on the datum line) × LC. Example: 5 mm + 37 × 0.01 mm = 5.37 mm.

**Zero error.** With the jaws closed: if a small division number n is on the datum line the error is **+ n × 0.01 mm** (subtract it); if a number close to 100, say 94, is on the datum line the error is **−(100 − 94) × 0.01 = −0.06 mm** (add it).

Only pictorial readings are asked in this course. Always close the jaws with the ratchet, not by turning the thimble hard.

key_terms.definition_md: The distance moved by the spindle of a screw gauge in one complete turn of the thimble.

sections.heading: 5. The simple pendulum
sections.body_md:
A **simple pendulum** is a small, heavy bob suspended by a light, inextensible thread from a rigid support. Its **effective length** *l* is the distance from the point of suspension to the **centre of the bob**.

**Time period T** is the time taken for one **complete oscillation**; **frequency f** is the number of oscillations per second, so **f = 1/T** (unit hertz, Hz). To find T accurately, time **20 oscillations** and divide by 20: this reduces the error because the stopwatch's least count is spread over 20 oscillations.

For small swings, **T = 2π √(l/g)** (stated without derivation). So T depends only on l and g: it does **not** depend on the mass of the bob. If l becomes 4 times, T doubles; at a place where g is smaller, T is larger.

**l against T² graph.** Squaring, T² = (4π²/g) l, so a graph of l (y-axis) against T² (x-axis) is a straight line through the origin with **slope = g ÷ 4π²**. Hence **g = 4π² × slope**; with the slope 0.25 m s⁻² and π = 3.14, g = 9.86 m s⁻². Choose a large right-angled triangle on the line to read the slope. Calculations use g = 10 m s⁻² and π = 3.14 unless the question says 9.8.

The distance from the point of suspension to the centre of the bob.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing the SI unit of mass as the gram; it is the kilogram.
- Forgetting that 1 g cm⁻³ is 1000 kg m⁻³, or dividing instead of multiplying.
- Counting marks instead of divisions when finding a least count.
- Adding a positive zero error (it is subtracted) or subtracting a negative one (it is added).
- Reading the main scale after the vernier zero instead of before it.
- Measuring the length of a pendulum to the top or bottom of the bob and not to its centre.
- Timing only one oscillation.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a unit, a definition or a single reading.
- 2 marks: a least count or a conversion with the factor shown.
- 3 marks: a reading with the main and vernier or circular parts and the zero-error correction.
- 10-mark structured question: set in parts on a figure or a table of readings. Write the formula, the substitution and the unit in every calculation and label graphs.

cards.front_md: Name the seven fundamental SI quantities.
cards.back_md: Length, mass, time, electric current, temperature, luminous intensity, amount of substance.

cards.front_md: SI units of current, temperature, luminous intensity and amount of substance?
cards.back_md: Ampere, kelvin, candela, mole.

cards.front_md: What is a derived unit?
cards.back_md: A unit made from fundamental units by following the formula of the quantity.

cards.front_md: Unit of density in fundamental units?
cards.back_md: kg m⁻³.

cards.front_md: Unit of momentum in fundamental units?
cards.back_md: kg m s⁻¹.

cards.front_md: Base units of the cgs system?
cards.back_md: Centimetre, gram, second.

cards.front_md: Base units of the fps system?
cards.back_md: Foot, pound, second.

cards.front_md: 1 g cm⁻³ in kg m⁻³?
cards.back_md: 1000 kg m⁻³.

cards.front_md: Convert km per hour to m per second.
cards.back_md: Multiply by 1000 and divide by 3600, that is divide by 3.6.

cards.front_md: 1 lb and 1 ft in SI?
Define least count.
cards.back_md: The smallest value that an instrument can measure accurately.

cards.front_md: Least count of a metre rule?
cards.back_md: 1 mm or 0.1 cm.

cards.front_md: How do you find the least count of a measuring cylinder?
cards.back_md: Volume between two marked values divided by the number of divisions between them.

cards.front_md: Why does a smaller least count mean greater accuracy?
cards.back_md: The possible error is a smaller fraction of the quantity measured.

cards.front_md: Where must the eye be when reading a measuring cylinder?
cards.back_md: Level with the bottom of the water meniscus.

cards.front_md: Least count of a Vernier callipers (10 VSD = 9 MSD, 1 MSD = 1 mm)?
Reading of a Vernier callipers?
cards.back_md: MSR + (coinciding vernier line) × LC.

cards.front_md: What is zero error?
cards.back_md: The reading shown when the instrument should read zero (jaws closed).

cards.front_md: Positive zero error: add or subtract?
cards.back_md: Subtract it: true reading = observed − zero error.

cards.front_md: Negative zero error of a Vernier callipers with the 8th line coinciding?
Pitch of a screw gauge?
cards.back_md: The distance the spindle moves in one full turn of the thimble.

cards.front_md: Least count of a screw gauge (pitch 1 mm, 100 divisions)?
Reading of a screw gauge?
cards.back_md: Linear scale reading + (circular division on the datum line) × LC.

cards.front_md: Use of the ratchet?
cards.back_md: It stops the spindle being tightened too much, so the wire is not squeezed.

cards.front_md: Zero error with division 94 on the datum line?
cards.back_md: −(100 − 94) × 0.01 = −0.06 mm; add 0.06 mm to the reading.

cards.front_md: Define time period and frequency of a pendulum.
cards.back_md: Time for one complete oscillation; number of oscillations per second; f = 1/T.

cards.front_md: Formula for the time period of a simple pendulum?
cards.back_md: T = 2π√(l/g) (no derivation needed).

cards.front_md: What does T not depend on?
cards.back_md: The mass of the bob (and, for small swings, the amplitude).

cards.front_md: Slope of the l against T² graph?
cards.back_md: g ÷ 4π², so g = 4π² × slope.

cards.front_md: Why time 20 oscillations instead of 1?
cards.back_md: The stopwatch error is shared among 20 oscillations, so T is more accurate.

questions.stem_md: Which one of the following is NOT a fundamental SI unit?
questions.solution_md: The newton is the unit of force, which is derived from kilogram, metre and second, so it is not fundamental, option (c).

questions.stem_md: A liquid has a density of 1.2 g cm⁻³. Its density in kg m⁻³ is
questions.solution_md: $1.2 \times 1000 = 1200$ kg m⁻³, option (b).

questions.stem_md: Between the 20 mL and the 30 mL marks of a measuring cylinder there are 5 equal divisions. Its least count is
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{30 - 20}{5} = 2$ mL, option (c).

questions.stem_md: A rule (least count 1 mm), a Vernier callipers (0.1 mm) and a screw gauge (0.01 mm) are used to measure the thickness of a coin. The most accurate value is given by
questions.solution_md: The smallest least count gives the smallest possible error, option (b).

questions.stem_md: In a Vernier callipers 10 vernier divisions are equal to 9 main scale divisions, and one main scale division is 1 mm. Its least count is
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{1\ \text{mm}}{10} = 0.1$ mm, option (c).

questions.stem_md: The spindle of a screw gauge moves 3 mm in 6 full turns of the thimble, which has 50 divisions. Its least count is
questions.solution_md: Pitch $= \dfrac{3}{6} = 0.5$ mm; least count $= \dfrac{0.5}{50} = 0.01$ mm, option (c).

questions.stem_md: The effective length of a simple pendulum is made 9 times as large at the same place. Its time period
questions.solution_md: $T \propto \sqrt{l}$, so $T$ changes by a factor $\sqrt{9} = 3$, option (a).

questions.stem_md: The slope of the straight line of an $l$ against $T^2$ graph of a simple pendulum is $0.25$ m s⁻². The value of $g$ is
questions.solution_md: Slope $= \dfrac{g}{4\pi^2}$, so $g = 4\pi^2 \times$ slope, option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is a fundamental physical quantity?
questions.solution_md: Electric current is one of the seven fundamental quantities; the other three are derived, option (c).

questions.stem_md: Momentum is the product of mass and velocity. Its SI unit in terms of fundamental units is
questions.solution_md: kg × (m s⁻¹) = kg m s⁻¹, option (d).

questions.stem_md: A school bus travels at 90 km h⁻¹ on an expressway. Its speed in m s⁻¹ is
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{90 \times 1000}{3600} = 25$ m s⁻¹, option (d).

questions.stem_md: The relation between the cgs and SI units of density is
questions.solution_md: A gram is 10⁻³ kg and a cm³ is 10⁻⁶ m³, so 1 g cm⁻³ = 1000 kg m⁻³, option (d).

questions.stem_md: The base units of the fps system of units are
questions.solution_md: The fps system uses the foot, the pound and the second, option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The ampere is a fundamental unit of the SI system.

**Reason (R):** The newton is a derived unit of the SI system.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true, but the newton being derived says nothing about why the ampere is fundamental, option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? In the cgs system the unit of mass is the gram and the unit of length is the centimetre.
questions.solution_md: True. The cgs system is centimetre, gram, second.

questions.stem_md: The SI units of electric current, temperature, luminous intensity and amount of substance are the ___, ___, ___ and ___ respectively.
questions.solution_md: Ampere, kelvin, candela and mole.

questions.stem_md: Name the unit of mass in the fps system.

answer.model_answer_md: The **pound**.

questions.solution_md: Pound.

questions.stem_md: A sheet of aluminium has a density of 2.7 g cm⁻³. Find its density in kg m⁻³.
A parcel weighs 20 lb. Find its mass in kg, to two decimal places. (1 lb = 0.4536 kg)
questions.solution_md: $20 \times 0.4536 = 9.07$ kg (9.072 rounded to two decimal places).

questions.stem_md: A boy is 5.5 ft tall. Find his height in cm. (1 ft = 30.48 cm)
Using the formulae density = mass ÷ volume and momentum = mass × velocity, write the SI units of density and momentum in terms of fundamental units.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Density:** kg ÷ m³ = **kg m⁻³**.

**Momentum:** kg × m s⁻¹ = **kg m s⁻¹**.

questions.solution_md: Follow each formula with kg, m and s.

questions.stem_md: A cyclist rides at 36 km h⁻¹. Convert this speed to m s⁻¹ and say whether it is a fundamental or a derived quantity.

answer.model_answer_md:
$36\ \text{km h}^{-1} = \dfrac{36 \times 1000}{3600} = 10$ m s⁻¹.

Speed is a **derived** quantity (distance ÷ time).

questions.solution_md: Divide by 3.6; speed is derived.

questions.stem_md: A steel rod has a density of 7.8 g cm⁻³ and a toy car has a mass of 250 g. (a) Express the density in kg m⁻³. (b) Express the mass of the toy car in kg. (c) Name the system of units in which the mass would be written in pounds.
questions.solution_md: Multiply by 1000; divide by 1000; fps.

questions.stem_md: The least count of an instrument is

options.text_md: the smallest value that it can measure accurately
the largest value that it can measure
the number of divisions on its scale
the full range of its scale

questions.solution_md: The least count is the smallest reading the instrument can give accurately, option (a).

The figure shows the water level in a measuring cylinder marked every 2 mL. The volume of water is
questions.solution_md: The level is 2 small divisions above 30 mL: 30 + 2 × 2 = 34 mL, option (b).

questions.stem_md: What is meant by the zero error of a Vernier callipers? State how a reading is corrected when the zero error is positive.

answer.model_answer_md: It is the reading shown by the instrument when the jaws are closed and should read zero. For a **positive** zero error, the error is **subtracted** from the observed reading.

questions.solution_md: Reading with the jaws closed; subtract a positive error.

questions.stem_md: A Vernier callipers has 10 vernier divisions equal to 9 main scale divisions, with 1 main division = 1 mm. (a) Find the length of one vernier division. (b) Hence find the least count in mm. (c) Why is a Vernier callipers preferred to a metre rule for measuring the diameter of a test tube?

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** 9 mm ÷ 10 = **0.9 mm**.

**(b)** Least count = 1 − 0.9 = **0.1 mm**.

**(c)** Its least count is 10 times smaller, so it measures the diameter **more accurately**.

questions.solution_md: 0.9 mm; 0.1 mm; smaller least count.

marking_scheme.step: More accurate because smaller least count

answer.model_answer_md: The pitch is the **distance moved by the spindle in one full turn** of the thimble. **Least count = pitch ÷ number of divisions on the circular scale.**

questions.stem_md: The figure shows a screw gauge (pitch 1 mm, 100 divisions) with its jaws closed. (a) State its zero error with the sign. (b) State whether the error is added to or subtracted from an observed reading. (c) State the use of the ratchet.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Division 97 is on the datum line, so the error is −(100 − 97) × 0.01 = **-0.03 mm**.

**(b)** A negative error is **added** to the observed reading.

**(c)** The ratchet **stops the spindle being tightened too much**, so the object is not squeezed.

questions.solution_md: −0.03 mm; added; avoids over-tightening.

questions.stem_md: Find the time period of a simple pendulum of effective length 0.40 m. (π = 3.14 and g = 10 m s⁻²)
questions.solution_md: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g}} = 2 \times 3.14 \times \sqrt{\dfrac{0.40}{10}} = 1.26$ s.

questions.stem_md: A seconds pendulum has a time period of 2 s. Find its effective length in m. (π = 3.14 and g = 10 m s⁻²)
questions.solution_md: $l = \dfrac{gT^2}{4\pi^2} = \dfrac{10 \times 4}{4 \times 3.14 \times 3.14} = 1.01$ m.

questions.stem_md: In an experiment on the simple pendulum why is the effective length measured up to the centre of the bob and not up to its top?

answer.model_answer_md: The bob swings as if all its mass were at its **centre**, so the thread alone is shorter than the true length. The distance to the centre is the **effective length used in the formula**.

questions.solution_md: Mass acts at the centre; formula uses that distance.

questions.stem_md: A student times one oscillation of a pendulum with a stopwatch of least count 0.1 s, and then times 20 oscillations. (a) Find the possible error in the period found from 20 oscillations. (b) State why timing 20 oscillations gives a more accurate period. (c) State the formula for the frequency in terms of the period.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Error in T = 0.1 ÷ 20 = **0.005 s**.

**(b)** The **same 0.1 s uncertainty is shared among 20 oscillations**, so the error in one period is 20 times smaller.

**(c)** f = **1 ÷ T**.

questions.solution_md: 0.005 s; shared error; f = 1/T.

questions.stem_md: State how the time period of a simple pendulum changes when (a) its effective length is made 4 times, (b) the mass of the bob is doubled, (c) the pendulum is taken to a place where g is smaller.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** T becomes **2 times** as large (T ∝ √l).

**(b)** **No change.**

**(c)** T **increases**, because T ∝ 1/√g.

questions.solution_md: Doubles; unchanged; increases.

questions.stem_md:
A student measures the diameter of a metal cylinder with a Vernier callipers in which 10 vernier divisions are equal to 9 main scale divisions, and one main scale division is 1 mm. Figure 1 shows the scales with the jaws closed. Figure 2 shows them with the cylinder held between the jaws.

(a) Calculate the least count of the instrument in cm. [2]

(b) State the zero error shown in Figure 1, with its sign. [2]

(c) Read the observed diameter from Figure 2. [3]

(d) Find the correct diameter of the cylinder. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Least count = 1 mm ÷ 10 = 0.1 mm = **0.01 cm**.

**(b)** The vernier zero is to the left of the main zero and the 8th line coincides, so the error is −(10 − 8) × 0.01 = **-0.02 cm**.

**(c)** Main scale reading = 45 mm; vernier reading = 3 × 0.1 = 0.3 mm; observed diameter = 45.3 mm = **4.53 cm**.

**(d)** The error is negative, so it is added: true diameter = 4.53 − (-0.02) = **4.55 cm**.

questions.stem_md:
A screw gauge has a pitch of 1 mm and 100 divisions on its circular scale. Figure 1 shows it with the jaws closed. Figure 2 shows a copper wire held between the jaws. (Take π = 3.14.)

(a) Calculate the least count of the screw gauge. [2]

(b) State the zero error shown in Figure 1, with its sign. [2]

(c) Read the observed diameter from Figure 2. [2]

(d) Find the correct diameter of the wire. [2]

(e) Find the area of cross-section of the wire in mm². [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Least count = pitch ÷ divisions = 1 ÷ 100 = **0.01 mm**.

**(b)** Division 4 is on the datum line, so the error is 4 × 0.01 = **+0.04 mm**.

**(c)** Linear scale 1 mm + 49 × 0.01 mm = **1.49 mm**.

**(d)** True diameter = 1.49 − 0.04 = **1.45 mm**.

**(e)** Radius = 1.45 ÷ 2 = 0.725 mm; area = πr² = 3.14 × 0.725 × 0.725 = **1.65 mm²**.

questions.stem_md:
A student measures the effective length l of a simple pendulum and the time period T for four lengths, and plots a graph of l (m) on the y-axis against T² (s²) on the x-axis, shown in the figure. (Take π = 3.14.)

(a) Define the time period of a simple pendulum. [1]

(b) Using T = 2π√(l/g), show that l is proportional to T² and write the slope of the graph in terms of g. [3]

(c) Use the points (2.5, 0.60) and (5.0, 1.20) on the line to find the slope, with its unit. [3]

(d) Hence find g, to two decimal places. [2]

(e) State one precaution in the experiment. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The **time taken for one complete oscillation** of the bob.

**(b)** Squaring, T² = 4π²l ÷ g, so **l = (g ÷ 4π²) T²**; l is proportional to T² and the **slope = g ÷ 4π²**.

**(c)** Slope = (1.20 − 0.60) ÷ (5.0 − 2.5) = **0.24 m s⁻²**.

**(d)** g = 4π² × slope = 4 × 3.14 × 3.14 × 0.24 = **9.47 m s⁻²**.

**(e)** Use a **small angle of swing** (less than about 10 degrees), or time 20 oscillations.

questions.solution_md: Definition; slope = g/4π²; 0.24 m s⁻²; 9.47 m s⁻².

questions.stem_md:
A student wants to measure the diameter of a thin wire, which is about 0.85 mm. She has a metre rule (least count 1 mm), a Vernier callipers (least count 0.1 mm) and a screw gauge (least count 0.01 mm).

(a) Define least count. [2]

(b) For each instrument find the least count as a percentage of 0.85 mm, to the nearest whole number for the first two and one decimal place for the third. [3]

(c) Name the most suitable instrument and give a reason. [2]

(d) The screw gauge has a pitch of 0.5 mm and 50 divisions on the circular scale. Show that its least count is 0.01 mm. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The **smallest value that an instrument can measure accurately**; for a scale it is the value of one smallest division.

**(b)** Rule: 1 ÷ 0.85 × 100 = **118%**; Vernier: 0.1 ÷ 0.85 × 100 = **12%**; screw gauge: 0.01 ÷ 0.85 × 100 = **1.2%**.

**(c)** The **screw gauge**, because its least count is the smallest, so the possible error is only about 1.2% of the diameter.

**(d)** Least count = pitch ÷ divisions = 0.5 ÷ 50 = **0.01 mm**.

questions.solution_md: Definition; 118%, 12%, 1.2%; screw gauge; 0.5/50 = 0.01 mm.
